vignette:
At eighteen, Leo Tran had already been a photographer for three years when he enlisted, his camera always slung across his chest like a second skin. He had believed he was documenting something important, that his images would tell the truth about what happened overseas. That belief had not survived his deployment. What survived instead was a single afternoon in a dusty village compound, when the Humvee ahead of him hit an IED and the world became a wall of sound and light and then a terrible silence. He had been the one with the camera. He had been the one who could see. And in the seconds after the blast, as he scrambled toward the wreckage, he had seen the driver’s face—a young man named Reyes who had taught him how to field-strip his rifle—and had known, with a clarity that still visited him without warning, that Reyes was already gone. Leo had kept moving. He had pulled at twisted metal, had shouted for a medic, had done everything a person was supposed to do. But what he remembered now, what came back to him more vividly than any ordinary memory had ever come, was the feeling of Reyes’s hand going slack in his own. That moment was not a memory in the way other memories were. It was brighter, louder, more real. When it surfaced—and it surfaced constantly, triggered by the crack of a car backfiring, the slam of a door, the sudden hiss of a pressure cooker in his mother’s kitchen—Leo did not simply recall it. He was there again, his palms slick with heat and dust, his throat raw from screaming.

Since returning home, Leo had come to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere. His old friends from high school talked about college applications and dorm room decorations, and he sat among them feeling like a ghost, a person who had seen something they could not see and could never unsee. He had also become certain that people could not be trusted. This was not a general suspicion; it was a felt truth, lodged somewhere deep. Strangers on the street, cashiers, even his own mother—he watched them all with a vigilance that exhausted him. He knew, rationally, that no one here was trying to harm him, but his body did not know that. His body was still over there. He jumped at the sound of a dropped pan, at the sudden bark of a dog, at the hum of a ceiling fan that sounded, for a split second, like something else entirely. And when he jumped, the rage came. It came hot and fast, a fury that had no target but demanded one. He had failed to protect Reyes. He had been right there, and he had not been enough. That failure was a fact he carried like a stone in his chest, and remembering it—which happened multiple times a day, without warning, without mercy—filled him with a rage that frightened him more than the fear did.

Leo had tried to manage this on his own. He stopped going to the grocery store because the fluorescent lights buzzed at a frequency that reminded him of something he could not name. He stopped answering calls from his old unit because their voices pulled him back. He took more assignments as a photographer—portraits, weddings, real estate listings—but found that he could not relax even in the safest spaces. A quiet studio, a client’s living room, his own bedroom: none of them felt safe. His body stayed coiled, waiting. And so he had started taking risks. He drove too fast on winding roads, not because he wanted to die but because the speed drowned out the noise in his head. He stopped wearing his seatbelt. He picked fights with strangers in parking lots, knowing it was stupid, doing it anyway, because the adrenaline was the only thing that made the world feel real instead of like a dream he was trapped inside. His mother had noticed. She had found him standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, staring at the knife block, and had asked him, in a voice he had not heard since he was a child, what he was doing. He had not known how to answer.

What finally brought Leo to a clinic was not the rage or the sleeplessness or the driving. It was a job. A wedding shoot in a park, which should have been simple. But a child had popped a balloon nearby, and Leo had dropped his camera, had hit the ground, had covered his head. The bride had stared at him. The groom had asked if he was okay. Leo had packed his equipment and left without a word, and he had known, driving home with his hands shaking on the wheel, that he could not keep living like this. He was afraid of what he might do next. He was afraid that the next time the memory came, he would not come back from it. But underneath that fear, there was something else: a small, stubborn hope that maybe, if he could find a way to stop running, he might finally be able to put the camera down without feeling like he was abandoning someone all over again.
